messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 74
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Editor
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 77

# The Weight of Quiet Rooms

Raymond is a 74-year-old Māori man who spent the better part of four decades shaping other people's words for a living. He worked his way up from a junior copy editor at a regional newspaper in Wellington to a senior editorial role at a respected publishing house, a career defined by his attention to what lies beneath the surface of language — what a writer means but cannot quite say. It is not lost on him, he admits quietly, that he has spent years helping others find their voice while remaining almost entirely silent about what happened to him.

The abuse began gradually, the way he says most terrible things do — so slowly that by the time he understood what was happening, it had already become the shape of his life. His marriage to Diane lasted eleven years. The physical violence started in the third year, following the loss of a pregnancy. He remembers the first time she struck him with something — a ceramic mug, across the shoulder — and how he stood very still afterward, more confused than hurt, telling himself it was grief, that she was not herself. He did not leave for another eight years. He is still working out why.

The violence escalated across those years in cycles he learned to read the way he reads a manuscript — looking for the signs, the shifts in tone, the pressure building beneath the surface. He developed a kind of hypervigilance he mistook for competence. He thought he was managing things. What he was actually doing, he now understands, was surviving.

The divorce was finalised when Raymond was 58. He moved into a small flat in Auckland and threw himself back into his work, editing longer hours than ever, grateful for the noise of other people's stories filling his head. For a time, it seemed to work. He functioned. He socialised carefully, at a distance. He did not speak of Diane to anyone.

The intrusions began in earnest after he retired at 70. Without the manuscripts to absorb him, the memories moved in like weather. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, his heart hammering, the sheets damp. Sometimes he is back in the kitchen of the house in Karori, bracing himself against the counter. Sometimes he does not know where he is for several seconds, and those seconds are the worst. He has taken to sleeping with a lamp on, something he finds quietly humiliating.

During the day he avoids the suburb where they lived, will not drive past certain streets. He cannot watch films in which a man is struck or cornered — he leaves the room without explanation, then sits with the shame of having left. He keeps his flat meticulously ordered, every object in its place, a control he understands intellectually but cannot relinquish. Loud voices from neighbouring apartments send a cold alertness through him that does not settle for hours.

He describes feeling hollowed out in a way that is difficult to articulate — a persistent numbness that lifts occasionally but never fully departs. He has grown estranged from his adult children, not through any rupture but through a slow withdrawal he initiated and now regrets but does not know how to reverse. He tells himself they are busy. He does not tell himself the truth, which is that closeness frightens him now in ways it did not before.

What troubles Raymond most, he says, is not the nightmares or the hypervigilance or even the loneliness. It is the belief, persistent and corrosive, that he should have known better. That a man his age, an educated man, a man who reads people for a living, should have seen it clearly and left sooner. He edits this belief occasionally, crosses it out, writes something kinder in the margin. But it keeps returning to the page.
